asBirthCard.p: This card comes from your birthdate, and it has nothing to do with the signs you were born under. Add up every digit of the date, keep adding until you're at 22 or under, and yours came to ten, whether it got there straight away or by way of 28, 37, 46 or 55. Ten is a funny number when you think about it. It's the last one you can count on your fingers and the first one that needs two digits, a one with a nought after it, so it's an ending and a fresh start written in the same spot. The Hermit comes just before it, a man on his own up a mountain with a lantern. Then the Wheel, and suddenly everything's moving again and there are other people in it. After it comes Justice, who weighs up what the turning did. The Wheel belongs to Jupiter, the planet that makes things bigger, and that's the nature of this card. It swells whatever it lands on, the good years and the rough ones both.

Mostly it shows up as a life with chapters you can name. Someone at a party asks how you ended up in your line of work and the answer has a twist in it, a job you took because a friend dropped out, a flat you got because the other applicant moved to Perth. You tend to notice when something's come round again. It's March and you think, hang on, it was March last time the money went sideways too. On a Sunday with nothing planned you're fine for about an hour, and then you're looking at flights or moving the couch to the other wall, because a completely flat week makes you itchy. And when a message turns up from someone you haven't heard from in six years, it doesn't surprise you much. People drift back into your life. You half expect it.

Luck is the gift everyone mentions with this card. The one underneath it is that you're very good company for someone who's hit the bottom. A friend loses the job or the marriage, and most people either go quiet or start handing out advice. You tend to sit down with them and talk about the time it happened to you, how long it took, and what came after. They believe you because you've actually been there, usually more than once. The same thing makes you steady when a workplace gets restructured or the family business has a terrible year. You've watched things drop and come back, so you don't panic, and the people around you borrow some of that calm without quite knowing where it came from. It gets remembered, too, sometimes years later.

The less obvious trouble is what you do when things are going well. Stability can feel a bit suspicious to a ten. The job's good, the relationship's fine, the rent's paid, and some part of you starts waiting for the drop, and occasionally, to be honest, gives the wheel a shove yourself so at least you picked the moment. You quit the good job. You start a fight on a quiet weekend. Jupiter's in there too, and in a good stretch it makes you generous in ways that cost later, the round of drinks for the whole table, the bigger lease, saying yes to three projects because you can't imagine ever being tired. Then the turn comes and you're stretched thin. It's worth noticing when you get twitchy in a calm patch, and asking yourself what you're actually bracing for.

When something goes wrong, the first thing you usually do is move. You make a big call fast, book the trip, hand in the notice, cut your hair, start looking at houses in another town, because doing anything feels better than sitting at the bottom waiting. A week later the adrenaline's gone and the second phase kicks in, which is going over it again and again for the exact moment it turned, the email you should have sent, the sign you missed. You start reading meaning into small things. For the people around you the hard part is the whiplash. Your partner agreed to the big change on Monday, and by Friday you're wondering aloud if it was a mistake. What helps is holding off on any decision you can't undo for a fortnight, and keeping the ordinary things going, the same breakfast, the same walk, the Thursday call with your sister.

You often meet people at a hinge, just after a move or a breakup or a new job, and the relationship gets tied up with that phase of your life. Which is lovely until the phase ends. The job changes or you move again, and you catch yourself wondering if the relationship belonged to the old chapter, when really it's just the first time the two of you have had to be ordinary together. Partners who need things steady can find you a bit hard to settle with, because they can feel you watching the horizon. You also tend to remember the dates of things, the first dinner, the night it nearly ended. It helps to tell a partner plainly when you're in a restless patch, so they don't take it as being about them. Usually it isn't.

You do well in work that runs in seasons, or in cycles you can see coming. Retail and hospitality, events, farming, teaching with its terms, sales with its quarters, anything where the end of the financial year actually matters. You're often good in a turnaround, the shop that's had a bad year or the team nobody wants to take on, because to you a low point is somewhere things start from. Where you struggle is the long flat middle of a project, month nine of eighteen, when nothing's changing and nobody's saying thanks. That's usually when the job ads come out. Money for a ten tends to arrive in waves, fat quarters and thin ones, especially if you work for yourself. The habit worth building is moving a fixed slice into a separate account in the good months, before Jupiter finds a use for it.

At twenty a lot happens to a ten that they didn't choose. A parent moves the family interstate, a course gets cancelled, someone leaves. It can feel like being thrown about, and plenty of tens go through a stretch of believing they're just unlucky. By the mid-thirties there's usually enough history to see the shape of it, and often a moment of realising that the worst year turned out to be where the good part started. After that you tend to get calmer about the drops and a little more careful at the peaks. The fifties often bring a kind of ease. You've been round enough times that neither the top nor the bottom feels personal any more, and people start ringing you when their own lives tip over, because you've seen it before.

Next time you're in a bad patch and lying awake over it, open the calendar on your phone and make an event three months out. Put the worry in the title in plain words, 'still no job?' or 'are we OK?', and leave it there. When it pops up, read it and see where things actually got to. Do it every time something drops. After a few of them you've got your own record of how things tend to move for you, in your own words, and you can scroll back through it.
